# Anthropic in Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode

Anthropic serves Claude on its Messages API, at `api.anthropic.com`. Add an Anthropic API key to magpie once, and Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and every other agent you connect can use Claude models through magpie’s local gateway at `127.0.0.1:3425`, each agent with a model of its own. Agents that speak another API are translated on the way.

## Add Anthropic

1. **Get a key.** Make one on [console.anthropic.com](https://console.anthropic.com/settings/keys). An API key starts with `sk-ant-api`.
2. **Add the provider.** In magpie’s Providers tab, press ＋ Add provider, pick Anthropic, paste the key and save. magpie asks Anthropic which models the key can use.
3. **Pick it for an agent.** In the Agents tab, click the model on the agent’s row and choose a Claude model such as `claude-opus-5-5`.

```
magpie provider add anthropic <key>
magpie provider test anthropic
```

Model ids in magpie are `provider/model`, so Anthropic’s read `anthropic/claude-opus-5-5`: the provider, then Anthropic’s own id. The key is kept in magpie’s settings; magpie doesn’t take it from your shell.

Already set Anthropic up in OpenCode or Alma? magpie’s import from those apps brings it in as the Anthropic provider.

This page is about an API key. A Claude Pro or Max subscription is signed in to separately; see [Subscriptions in any agent](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/subscriptions).

## Endpoints

| API | Address | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Messages | `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages` | every agent’s requests: Claude Code’s as sent, Codex’s, Gemini CLI’s and OpenCode’s translated |
| Models | `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/models` | the model list |

magpie’s Anthropic provider has no Chat Completions or Responses address, so an agent that speaks either, or Google’s Gemini API, is translated to Messages and the reply translated back, streaming and tool calls included.

## Model list

magpie fetches the list from Anthropic, at `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/models`, every page of it, so agents see the models your key can use. Names, context windows and prices come from models.dev’s `anthropic` catalog. Pick the models agents see in the provider’s model list, or from the terminal:

```
magpie provider models anthropic +claude-opus-5-5 +claude-sonnet-5-5 +claude-haiku-5-5
magpie provider refresh-every anthropic 1d
```

Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 take 1M tokens. On a window that long, Codex compacts a conversation at 272K rather than send ever more of it on every turn; `magpie model compact off` lets it run to the whole window. In Claude Code a Claude model runs to its own window, as Anthropic runs it: 200K unless a `[1m]` one is picked.

## In each agent

```
magpie claude anthropic/claude-opus-5-5
magpie codex anthropic/claude-opus-5-5
magpie gemini model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5
magpie opencode anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5
```

- **Claude Code.** speaks Anthropic Messages, so its requests go to Anthropic as Claude Code sent them, its own cache marks, thinking and betas included, with the fixes below. [Models in Claude Code](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/claude-code-models).
- **Codex.** speaks OpenAI Responses, which Anthropic doesn’t serve. magpie translates each request to Messages and the reply back, marks the prompt for Anthropic’s cache, and keeps Claude’s signed thinking across a tool loop. [Models in Codex](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/codex-models).
- **Gemini CLI.** speaks Google’s Gemini API. magpie translates each request to Messages and the reply back. [Models in Gemini CLI](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/gemini-cli-models).
- **OpenCode.** speaks Chat Completions to magpie, so its requests are translated to Messages too. [Models in OpenCode](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/opencode-models).

## What magpie does for Anthropic

A request magpie translates is built the way Anthropic’s Messages API wants it, and a few things Anthropic would refuse are fixed on Claude Code’s requests too:

- **Prompt caching..** Anthropic caches a prompt only up to a block marked with `cache_control`, and a request from another API has no marks. magpie marks the system prompt (or the last tool, when there is no system prompt) and the conversation’s last block, two marks at most, so the next turn reads what came before from the cache. A request that brings `cache_control` of its own keeps its marks, and magpie adds none.
- **An hour’s cache for Codex..** Codex’s turns are often more than five minutes apart, so the marks magpie adds to its requests last an hour, unless Codex asks `prompt_cache_retention` `in_memory`. An upstream that turns the hour’s `ttl` away is asked again with five-minute marks, and magpie remembers it.
- **Signed thinking..** Claude signs its thinking and wants it back on a tool loop’s next turn. Codex gets each thinking block, signature included, in its reasoning item’s `encrypted_content`, and magpie sends it back to Anthropic as it was; redacted thinking goes back sealed. Thinking with no signature is left out, and so is thinking another vendor signed, such as DeepSeek’s earlier in a routing group, which Claude refuses.
- **Tool calls..** A call an interrupted turn left unanswered gets a result saying it is unavailable, and a result for a call Anthropic never saw becomes text, where Anthropic would refuse the request. A history with calls but no tools declared declares them, with `tool_choice` none. A required tool goes as `any`, a named one as `tool`, and parallel calls turned off as `disable_parallel_tool_use`.
- **Sampling..** Opus 4.7 and later, Sonnet 5 and 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5 refuse `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k`, which Claude Code’s auto mode classifier sends. magpie leaves them out for those models.
- **Betas..** The betas an agent asks in `anthropic-beta` go on to Anthropic, save Claude Code’s own sign-in beta (`oauth-…`), which names a credential that never leaves magpie.
- **Structured output..** A request for JSON in a schema goes to Anthropic as `output_config.format`.

## Reasoning

- **Effort..** Claude models from 4.6 on think adaptively. A translated request’s effort goes as `output_config.effort`, with thinking adaptive and its summary shown (`display: summarized`), since Opus 4.7 and later leave the thinking text out unless asked. Opus and Sonnet 4.6 have no xhigh, so xhigh is asked as max.
- **Budgets..** Older Claude models get a thinking budget: 4,096 tokens at low, 10,000 at medium, 24,000 at high, 32,000 at xhigh and max, fitted under the request’s `max_tokens`.
- **A budget to a newer model..** A request with a thinking budget to a model from 4.6 on, which Claude Opus 5.5 refuses (“requires adaptive thinking”), goes as adaptive thinking, the budget asked as the nearest effort.
- **Reasoning off..** Codex’s or a Chat client’s effort none turns thinking off, not down to a low budget. Each model takes off its own way: Sonnet 5.5 is sent `between_tools`, an effort above high asked as high; Opus 5.5 and Fable 5 always think, so thinking is left out; Opus 5 and Haiku 5.5 are asked high in place of xhigh or max; older Claudes take it as sent. Claude Code’s requests with thinking off are fitted the same way.

## Web search

Anthropic searches the web itself. Claude Code’s WebSearch goes to Anthropic as it is. When Codex, Gemini CLI or a Chat client asks to search, magpie offers Claude Anthropic’s own `web_search_20250305` tool, up to five searches a request, rather than magpie’s searcher.

## Cost and usage

- **Cache tokens..** The Usage tab counts cache reads, five-minute cache writes and hour-long cache writes apart from the rest of the prompt, as Anthropic reports them.
- **Cost..** The Usage tab prices each call with Anthropic’s prices from models.dev. An hour-long write is priced at twice the input price where the catalog gives none, as Anthropic bills it. magpie reads no balance from Anthropic; type it in with `key-balance`, and the Usage page shows it less what magpie has priced the key’s calls at since.
- **Keeping the cache..** With several keys, a conversation stays on its key while its cache is worth keeping, 1,024 tokens or more, and still warm: read within the last five minutes, or within the hour when it was written for an hour.

## Several keys and failover

One Anthropic provider can hold several keys: press Add another key under it, or paste several at once. Requests go to the first key that’s on, and when it runs out or is rate limited the next one takes over.

- **Spend caps..** `spend-cap` stops a key at a dollar amount a day, a month or in all, as the Usage tab prices its calls; routing then goes on to the other keys and the fallbacks.
- **Fallbacks..** `fallback` names where requests go when Anthropic is out of quota or down: another provider’s model or a routing group.
- **Workspaces..** A key that reaches several workspaces names the one each request is for with the `anthropic-workspace-id` header. Add the provider again under an id of its own, with the header set in its Headers field or from the terminal; its models then read `anthropic-ws2/…`.

```
magpie provider spend-cap anthropic <key> 20 month
magpie provider key-balance anthropic <key> 25
magpie provider fallback anthropic deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
magpie provider add anthropic <key> id=anthropic-ws2 name="Anthropic WS2" header.anthropic-workspace-id=wrkspc_…
```

## Troubleshooting

- **“requires adaptive thinking”..** A thinking budget sent to a model from 4.6 on. magpie sends it as adaptive thinking with the nearest effort; see Reasoning.
- **400 when thinking is turned off..** Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5 each refuse `disabled`, and Opus 5 and Haiku 5.5 refuse it at xhigh and max. magpie sends each model off the way it takes it.
- **“`temperature` is deprecated for this model”..** magpie leaves `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` out for the models that refuse them.
- **“`tool_use` ids were found without `tool_result` blocks”..** An interrupted turn left a call unanswered. In a request magpie translates, the call gets a result saying it is unavailable.
- **“Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block”..** The conversation ran on another vendor first. magpie leaves thinking another vendor signed, or left unsigned, out of what goes to Claude.
- **A 400 about `cache_control` and `ttl`..** The upstream doesn’t take the hour-long marks magpie adds for Codex. magpie asks again with five-minute marks and keeps to them for that provider.
- **“this is an Anthropic API key, not a setup-token”..** The key went to the Claude subscription’s sign-in. Add it as the Anthropic provider instead.
- **Checking a key..** `magpie provider test anthropic` sends a tiny request through each endpoint, or to each model you name. Add `--as codex` or `--as claude-code` to send it the way that agent would.

## FAQ

### How do I use an Anthropic API key in Claude Code?

Add your Anthropic API key in magpie (Providers, Add provider, Anthropic), then pick a Claude model such as `claude-opus-5-5` on Claude Code’s row, or run `magpie claude anthropic/claude-opus-5-5`. Claude Code speaks Anthropic Messages, so its requests go to `https://api.anthropic.com` as it sent them, with what the model would refuse fixed on the way.

### Can Codex use Claude models?

Yes. Codex speaks OpenAI Responses, which Anthropic doesn’t serve, so magpie translates each request to the Messages API and the reply back. It marks the prompt for Anthropic’s cache with marks that last an hour, and keeps Claude’s signed thinking across a tool loop in Codex’s `encrypted_content`. Run `magpie codex anthropic/claude-opus-5-5`.

### How do I use Claude in OpenCode through magpie?

Pick the model in magpie, or run `magpie opencode anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5`. OpenCode speaks Chat Completions to magpie, so magpie translates its requests to Anthropic’s Messages API, marks the prompt for the cache and fits the reasoning effort to the model.

### Can Gemini CLI use Claude?

Yes. Gemini CLI speaks Google’s Gemini API, so magpie translates its requests to Anthropic’s Messages API and the replies back, streaming and tool calls included. Run `magpie gemini model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5`.

### Does magpie keep Anthropic’s prompt cache for agents it translates?

Yes. A request from Codex, Gemini CLI or OpenCode has no cache marks of its own, so magpie marks the system prompt and the conversation’s last block, two marks at most, and the next turn reads what came before from the cache. A request that brings its own `cache_control` keeps its marks. Codex’s marks last an hour, the rest five minutes.

### Why does Claude answer 400 when thinking is turned off?

Newer Claude models don’t all take `thinking` `disabled`. magpie sends Sonnet 5.5 `between_tools`, leaves thinking out for Opus 5.5 and Fable 5, which always think, and asks Opus 5 and Haiku 5.5 at high in place of xhigh or max. Older Claudes get it as sent.

**By provider:** [DeepSeek](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/deepseek) · [Kimi and Kimi Code](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/kimi) · [GLM Coding Plan](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/glm) · [Qwen](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/qwen) · [MiniMax](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/minimax) · [OpenAI](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/openai) · [Gemini](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/gemini) · [Grok](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/grok) · [Mistral](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/mistral) · [OpenRouter](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/openrouter) · [GitHub Copilot](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/copilot) · [Ollama](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/ollama)

Every agent: [Models in Claude Code](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/claude-code-models), [Models in Codex](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/codex-models), [Models in Gemini CLI](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/gemini-cli-models), [Models in OpenCode](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/opencode-models). Ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF) if you get stuck.

# OpenAI in Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode

OpenAI serves its models on two APIs at `api.openai.com`: Responses and Chat Completions. Its own models are best asked on Responses, and its newest answer only there. Add an OpenAI API key to magpie once, and Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and every other agent you connect can use OpenAI’s models through magpie’s local gateway at `127.0.0.1:3425`, each agent with a model of its own. Codex’s requests go to OpenAI as they are; the other agents’ are translated on the way.

This page is about an API key from platform.openai.com. A ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription is signed in to separately; see [Subscriptions in any agent](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/subscriptions).

## Add OpenAI

1. **Get a key.** Make one on [platform.openai.com](https://platform.openai.com/api-keys). It starts with `sk-`.
2. **Add the provider.** In magpie’s Providers tab, press ＋ Add provider, pick OpenAI, paste the key and save. magpie asks OpenAI which models the key can use.
3. **Pick it for an agent.** In the Agents tab, click the model on the agent’s row and choose an OpenAI model such as `gpt-6.1-sol`.

```
magpie provider add openai <key>
magpie provider test openai
```

Model ids in magpie are `provider/model`, so OpenAI’s read `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`: the provider, then OpenAI’s own id. The key is kept in magpie’s settings; magpie doesn’t take it from your shell.

Already set OpenAI up in OpenCode or another app magpie imports from? The import brings it in as the OpenAI provider.

## Endpoints

| API | Address | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Responses | `https://api.openai.com/v1` | OpenAI’s own models, ids starting `gpt-`, `codex` or `o` and a digit: Codex’s requests as they are, Claude Code’s, Gemini CLI’s and OpenCode’s translated |
| Chat Completions | `https://api.openai.com/v1` | the model list, and any other model the key lists |

magpie’s OpenAI provider has no Anthropic Messages address, so Claude Code’s requests are always translated. For OpenAI’s own models magpie keeps Responses first even for an agent that speaks Chat Completions. When OpenAI answers that a model is served only on `/v1/responses`, magpie asks again there and remembers it. To send a model on one API yourself:

```
magpie model api openai/gpt-5.5 chat
magpie model api openai/gpt-5.5 --reset
magpie model apis openai
```

**Azure OpenAI** is a provider of its own, Azure OpenAI. Give it your resource’s endpoint, `https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`, and its key. magpie uses the v1 API under `/openai/v1` for Chat Completions and Responses, sends the key in the `api-key` header, and lists the resource’s deployments as its models. A deployment named for its model, such as `gpt-5-codex`, goes to Responses first too.

## Model list

magpie fetches the list from OpenAI, at `https://api.openai.com/v1/models`, so agents see the models your key can use. Names, context windows, reasoning levels and prices come from models.dev’s `openai` catalog. A reasoning model OpenAI has just listed, before its levels are known, gets those of the newest reasoning model in its family: `gpt-6.1-sol` got `gpt-6-sol`’s. Pick the models agents see in the provider’s model list, or from the terminal:

```
magpie provider models openai +gpt-6.1-sol +gpt-6-luna +gpt-5.5
magpie provider refresh-every openai 1d
```

## In each agent

```
magpie claude openai/gpt-6.1-sol
magpie codex openai/gpt-6.1-sol
magpie gemini model openai/gpt-6.1-sol
magpie opencode openai/gpt-6.1-sol
```

- **Claude Code.** speaks Anthropic Messages, which OpenAI doesn’t serve. magpie translates each request to Responses and the reply back; the model’s reasoning summary reaches Claude Code as thinking, then the text. [Models in Claude Code](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/claude-code-models).
- **Codex.** speaks Responses, so its requests go to OpenAI as they are: its custom tools such as `apply_patch`, its reasoning items and its own `prompt_cache_key` included. Codex is also offered Fast here; see Reasoning. [Models in Codex](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/codex-models).
- **Gemini CLI.** speaks Google’s Gemini API. magpie translates each request to Responses and the reply back. [Models in Gemini CLI](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/gemini-cli-models).
- **OpenCode.** speaks Chat Completions. OpenAI’s own models go to Responses first, so magpie translates its requests there and the replies back; any other model the key lists gets OpenCode’s requests as they are. [Models in OpenCode](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/opencode-models).

## What magpie does for OpenAI

- **A prompt cache key..** A translated request to OpenAI that carries no `prompt_cache_key` gets one, made from the session the agent names, or else its first user message, and hashed, so it names nothing of the agent. Codex sends its own, which goes on as it is, and one you set yourself wins. If OpenAI answers 400 over the field, magpie asks again without it.
- **Tools loaded where they were loaded..** A tool that Claude Code’s tool search loads mid-conversation is sent to OpenAI’s Responses API as an `additional_tools` item at that point, not added to the tool list, which keeps the cached prefix. `additional-tools=off` puts it with the other tools.
- **Sealed reasoning from elsewhere..** OpenAI reads only its own sealed reasoning (`encrypted_content`). An item sealed under another key, organization or account is refused (“could not be verified”); magpie asks again without those items and remembers it for the conversation. Claude’s thinking, which Codex carries in a reasoning item after a turn on a Claude model, is taken out before the request reaches OpenAI.
- **Earlier responses..** A Responses client may send only a turn’s new input and name the response it follows (`previous_response_id`). magpie keeps each response it gave such a client, in memory and under the caller’s gateway key. OpenAI keeps responses too, so when the same key answered the one named, OpenAI is sent only the new input after its own id. Codex over HTTP says `store` false and names none.
- **Codex’s own compaction..** With `compaction=native`, Codex’s compaction is asked of OpenAI as Codex sent it and the sealed item comes back to Codex as it came. Only the key that sealed it can read it, so later requests carrying it go only there. The default, `compaction=magpie`, has magpie summarise.

```
magpie provider set openai compaction=native
magpie provider set openai additional-tools=off
```

## Reasoning

- **Effort..** The effort an agent asks for is fitted to the nearest level the model has, as the catalog lists them: `gpt-6-sol` has `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`. On Responses it is sent as `reasoning.effort`, with `summary` set to `auto`, so the model’s reasoning summary comes back.
- **Reasoning off..** When an agent whose requests magpie translates, such as Gemini CLI, turns reasoning off and the model lists `none` among its levels, magpie asks for none.
- **Encrypted reasoning..** magpie passes on what an agent asks to include, but asks for `reasoning.encrypted_content` only with reasoning: OpenAI refuses it of a model that doesn’t reason. Codex sends the sealed items back on the next turn, and magpie passes them on as they are.
- **Fast..** On an OpenAI key, Codex is offered Fast for GPT and o-series models. magpie sends it as `service_tier: "priority"`, OpenAI’s priority processing. A service tier set for Codex in magpie overrides what Codex asked.

## Web search

OpenAI’s Responses API searches the web itself. When an agent offers its model web search, as Codex and Claude Code do, magpie gives the model OpenAI’s own `web_search` tool on Responses, and OpenAI runs the search.

## Cost and usage

- **Cost..** The Usage tab prices each call with OpenAI’s prices from models.dev.
- **Cache tokens..** When a reply reports cached prompt tokens, the Usage tab counts them apart from the rest of the prompt.
- **Keeping the cache..** With several keys, a conversation stays on its key while its cache is worth keeping, 1,024 tokens or more, and still warm, read within the last five minutes.
- **Service tier..** Each call records the tier the agent asked for, the one magpie sent, and the one OpenAI’s reply says it ran at.
- **Balance..** magpie reads no balance from OpenAI; type it in with `key-balance`, and the Usage page shows it less what magpie has priced the key’s calls at since.

## Several keys and failover

One OpenAI provider can hold several keys: press Add another key under it, or paste several at once. Requests go to the first key that’s on, and when it runs out or is rate limited the next one takes over. To keep keys apart instead, say from two organizations, add the provider again: the second is `openai-2`.

- **Spend caps..** `spend-cap` stops a key at a dollar amount a day, a month or in all, as the Usage tab prices its calls; routing then goes on to the other keys and the fallbacks.
- **Fallbacks..** `fallback` names where requests go when OpenAI is out of quota or down: another provider’s model or a routing group.

```
magpie provider spend-cap openai <key> 20 month
magpie provider key-balance openai <key> 25
magpie provider fallback openai deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
```

## Troubleshooting

- **“The encrypted content for item rs_… could not be verified”..** The conversation carries reasoning sealed under another key, organization or account. magpie asks again without those items; see What magpie does.
- **A model that answers only on `/v1/responses`..** magpie moves it to Responses and remembers it. `magpie model apis openai` shows which API each model is asked on.
- **A 400 over `prompt_cache_key`..** magpie asks again without the key it added.
- **Checking a key..** `magpie provider test openai` sends a tiny request through each endpoint, or to each model you name. Add `--as codex` or `--as claude-code` to send it the way that agent would.

## FAQ

### How do I use OpenAI’s models in Claude Code?

Add your OpenAI API key in magpie (Providers, Add provider, OpenAI), then pick a model such as `gpt-6.1-sol` on Claude Code’s row, or run `magpie claude openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. OpenAI serves no Anthropic Messages API, so magpie translates Claude Code’s requests to OpenAI’s Responses API at `https://api.openai.com/v1` and the replies back, the reasoning summary as thinking.

### Can Codex use an OpenAI API key instead of a ChatGPT sign-in?

Yes. Add the key, then run `magpie codex openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. Codex speaks Responses, so its requests go to OpenAI as they are, custom tools and reasoning included, and Fast is sent as priority processing. A ChatGPT Plus or Pro sign-in is set up separately, in Subscriptions.

### How do I use GPT models in OpenCode?

Pick the model in magpie, or run `magpie opencode openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. OpenCode speaks Chat Completions, but OpenAI’s own models go to Responses first, so magpie translates OpenCode’s requests there and the replies back. To send a model on Chat Completions instead, run `magpie model api openai/gpt-5.5 chat`.

### Can Gemini CLI use OpenAI?

Yes. Gemini CLI speaks Google’s Gemini API, so magpie translates its requests to OpenAI’s Responses API and the replies back, streaming and tool calls included. Run `magpie gemini model openai/gpt-6.1-sol`.

### Does magpie keep OpenAI’s prompt cache?

Yes. Codex’s own `prompt_cache_key` goes on as it is. A translated request without one gets a key made from its session or first user message, hashed so it names nothing of the agent. With several keys, a conversation stays on its key while its cache is warm.

### Why does OpenAI say the encrypted content could not be verified?

OpenAI reads only reasoning it sealed for the same key, organization or account. When a conversation carries reasoning sealed elsewhere, magpie asks again without those items and remembers it for the conversation.

### Does magpie support Azure OpenAI?

Yes, as its own provider, Azure OpenAI. Give it the resource’s endpoint and key; magpie uses the v1 API under `/openai/v1`, sends the key in the `api-key` header and lists the resource’s deployments as models.

**By provider:** [DeepSeek](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/deepseek) · [Kimi and Kimi Code](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/kimi) · [GLM Coding Plan](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/glm) · [Qwen](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/qwen) · [MiniMax](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/minimax) · [Anthropic](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/anthropic) · [Gemini](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/gemini) · [Grok](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/grok) · [Mistral](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/mistral) · [OpenRouter](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/openrouter) · [GitHub Copilot](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/copilot) · [Ollama](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/ollama)

Ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF) if you get stuck.

# Intent routing

Send a turn to a model by what the user asks for: tests to the strong model, quick questions to the fast cheap one. You describe each kind in a few words. When a turn begins, a small model you choose picks which kind the message is.

Intent is one of the conditions a [routing group’s rule](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/start#rules) can have, next to length, images, reasoning and agent. This page describes exactly what magpie does with it, as of v0.1.99, so you can predict every decision and check it in the Routing tab.

> **In one paragraph.** magpie decides once per turn: when you send a message, not while the agent works through tool calls. If a rule with an intent could be the first to match, magpie asks the group’s *classifier* model one short question through its own gateway. The question holds the intents as a numbered list plus the text of your latest message, and the classifier answers with a number. magpie reads that number and checks the rules top first with it. The first rule that matches puts its model first, and the group’s other models stay behind it for failover. The turn then stays on that model until you speak again. If the classifier fails, times out or answers something else, no intent matches and the turn is routed as if those rules weren’t there. There are no embeddings, no keyword lists and no training: the model you pick reads your message and picks a number.

## Set it up

You need a [routing group](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/start#routing) with at least two models, and one more model to classify with. The classifier can be any model magpie has, in the group or not.

1. **Open the group.** Go to Routing, find the group under *Routing groups* and click Edit.
2. **Add a rule with an intent.** Click Add a rule. The new rule reads asks for → a model, with the intent box ready: type what the message asks for, such as *writing or fixing tests*, then pick the model after →. More conditions come from the rule’s +, and must hold too.
3. **Pick the classifier.** Intent told by appears once a rule has an intent, set to Jev when you have a TypeSafe provider. Otherwise choose a small, fast model without reasoning. A group whose effort Jev already picks offers the same under its classifier: It can pick the model too. A group can’t be saved with an intent and no classifier.
4. **Save, and send a message.** Changes apply from the next turn, with no restart. The Routing tab shows what the classifier said and where the turn went.

The timeout is global: in Settings → Models → Replies → Intent classifier timeout, choose 8, 15, 30 or 60 seconds. It defaults to 8 seconds and applies to the next classifier call, including Jev, with no restart. A slow classifier may need longer, but the turn waits for it before routing. In `~/.config/magpie/settings.json`, `"classifyTimeout"` accepts whole seconds from 1 to 60; 0 or a missing field uses 8. A custom value in that range appears as its own choice in Settings.

The same from a terminal:

```
magpie group rule add coder use=deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash intent="a quick question" classifier=groq/llama-3.1-8b-instant
magpie group rule add coder use=deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro intent="writing or fixing tests"
magpie group rule add coder use=deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro use-effort=low intent="a simple edit"   # the same model, asked for low reasoning
magpie group rule coder                           # the rules, numbered, and the classifier
magpie group rule classifier coder groq/llama-3.1-8b-instant   # change the classifier
magpie group rule mv coder 3 1                    # order matters: top first
magpie group rule rm coder 2
```

`intent=` also takes the spellings `asks=` and `about=`. `classifier=` also takes `classify=` and `by=`. `classifier=` on `rule add` sets the group’s classifier and is needed only the first time. The classifier is saved in the group’s record in `~/.config/magpie/providers.json` as `"classifier"`, and each rule as `{"use": …, "intent": …}`.

A rule can also set the reasoning its model is asked for, so an intent picks the model and the effort as a pair: `use-effort=` (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`), saved as `"useEffort"`, such as `{"use": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro", "intent": "a simple edit", "useEffort": "low"}`. In the editor it is set from the rule’s ⋯ menu, Set its reasoning, and shows beside the model. The rule’s model is then asked for that effort on the turn’s requests, whatever the agent asked, at the model’s nearest level. A model whose levels magpie doesn’t know is asked as the agent asked, and so are the models the group fails over to. A model fixed at an effort in the group keeps its own. Without it, the model is asked as the agent asked. The Routing tab says when a rule set the effort.

## How a turn is routed

Every request an agent sends to a group with rules goes through these steps, in this order:

1. **Is this a new turn?.** magpie looks at the request’s last user message. If it carries text or an image and no tool result, you just spoke, so a new turn begins. If it carries tool results, the agent is continuing a turn already under way (see The rest of the turn). Turns are counted per conversation. A subagent is its own conversation: it shares its agent’s session but starts with different words.
2. **Which intents could decide?.** magpie walks the rules top first and ignores intent for now: a rule is a candidate if its other conditions (tokens, images, reasoning, agents) hold for this request. Each candidate’s intent is collected, and duplicates spelled the same apart from case count once. The walk stops at the first candidate *without* an intent, because that rule matches outright and nothing below it could come first. If no intents were collected, the classifier isn’t asked and costs nothing.
3. **Ask the classifier.** magpie sends the classifier the collected intents and the text of your message. The exact prompt is shown below. The call goes through magpie’s own gateway, like a request from an agent, so it uses that model’s provider with its keys or accounts and their failover. It has the configured timeout to answer (8 seconds by default).
4. **Read the answer.** magpie takes the first whole number in the reply. `1` to `n` names that intent, and `0` means none of them. Anything else, such as no number or one out of range, counts as a failure. The answer is kept for 10 minutes for the same message and intents.
5. **Match the rules.** The rules are checked top first with the answer. A rule with an intent matches only when the classifier named its intent, compared without case, and all its other conditions hold. The first rule that matches wins. If none matches, the group routes the turn as it always does.
6. **Order the models.** The winning rule’s model goes first, and the group’s other models follow in their usual order as failover. This holds even if another model answered the conversation’s last turn: a rule outranks the Stays setting as a turn begins. If the rule’s model has nothing ready right now (every key resting, the provider off), the group’s usual order stands and the trace says so.
7. **Remember the decision.** magpie keeps the decision for this conversation (the group, the agent’s session and the conversation’s first words) with the classifier’s answer, so the rest of the turn follows it.

### An example

The Coder group above has three rules:

| # | When | Send to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | ≥ 128000 tokens | kimi/kimi-k2.5 |
| 2 | asks for “a quick question” | deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash |
| 3 | asks for “writing or fixing tests” | deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro |

- A 20k-token turn: rule 1 doesn’t hold, so both intents are candidates. The classifier is asked to choose between “a quick question” and “writing or fixing tests”.
- A 150k-token turn: rule 1 has no intent and holds, so the walk stops there. The classifier isn’t asked, and the turn goes to Kimi.
- The classifier says `0` (none): no rule matches, and the turn goes by the group’s routing (here *In order*, so deepseek-v4-pro first).

### In the app

A real request through a group with two intent rules (“a quick question or explanation, with no code to write or change” and “writing or fixing tests”), sent from Claude Code: “Add unit tests for the LRU cache in cache.go, covering eviction and concurrent reads and writes”. The Routing tab shows it as it happens.

## What the classifier sees

This is the whole request, and nothing else is sent. The system message is fixed. The user message lists your intents in rule order, as they were collected in step 2:

```
You route a user's message to a coding assistant by what it asks for. Given numbered kinds of request and the user's message, answer with the number of the kind the message is, or 0 if it is none of them. Answer with the number only.
```

```
Kinds:
1. a quick question
2. writing or fixing tests

The user's message:
<message>
Write unit tests for the parseTokens function and fix any that fail.
</message>

The number of its kind (0 for none):
```

- **Only your latest message..** magpie sends the text parts of the last user message and nothing else: no earlier turns, no system prompt, no tool definitions, no files.
- **Images aren’t sent..** A message that is only an image has no words to classify, so no intent matches. To route by images, use the rule’s has an image condition.
- **Agent reminders are removed..** `<system-reminder>…</system-reminder>` blocks, which Claude Code adds to your message, are stripped. Other text an agent puts in the same message is kept.
- **Long messages are shortened..** Over 4,000 characters, magpie keeps the first 3,000 and the last 1,000, joined by `…`. The start and the end usually say what is being asked.
- **The request settings..** An OpenAI-style chat completion, not streamed, with `temperature 0`, `max_tokens 2048` and User-Agent `magpie-router/1`. When magpie knows the classifier’s reasoning levels, it asks for the least: `none` if the model has it, else its lowest level (for example `low`). When the levels aren’t known, nothing is sent and the vendor’s default applies. magpie translates it for the classifier’s provider, like any other request, so an Anthropic, Gemini or other model works too.

## When it can’t say

A classifier is a helper, not a gate. Whatever happens to it, the turn is still answered: the intent rules just don’t match.

| What happens | What magpie does |
| --- | --- |
| It answers `0` | No intent matches. Rules without an intent and the group’s usual order decide. |
| No answer within the configured timeout | Treated as a failure: no intent matches, and the turn goes on at once. |
| An error (quota, 5xx, bad key) | Its provider’s own failover is tried first, within the configured timeout. If it still fails, no intent matches. |
| An answer that isn’t a number from 0 to n | No intent matches this turn. The classifier did answer, so it isn’t rested: the next turn asks it again. |
| An error or a timeout | That classifier model is left alone for 30 s: turns in that time don’t wait on it, and the trace says it wasn’t asked. The first good answer clears this. |
| The message has no words | Not asked. No intent matches. |

Each case is written in the turn’s trace with the reason. An intent rule can therefore make a turn go to a different model than you hoped, but it can’t make it fail.

## The rest of the turn

A turn is often dozens of requests: the agent calls a tool, sends the result back, calls another, and so on. magpie deals with them like this:

- **Held..** Every request within the turn goes to the model the turn began on, and the classifier isn’t asked again. Switching models mid-turn would throw away what the vendor cached of the conversation (prompt caching), and some vendors reject reasoning that another one wrote.
- **Failover sticks..** If the rule’s model failed and another member answered, that member keeps the rest of the turn (with Stays on *Auto*, *Session* or *Within a turn*). The rule decides again at your next message.
- **Outgrown..** The one exception: if the conversation grows within the turn to 95% of the current model’s context, magpie checks the rules again, keeping the classifier’s earlier answer. If a rule sends it to a model with *more* context, it moves. It never moves to a model with less.
- **Waits..** If magpie didn’t see the turn begin (it was started or restarted in the middle of one), or the rule that decided it was removed or now sends to another model, no rule moves the turn. The rules decide again at your next message.
- **Subagents..** A subagent’s turns are decided on their own, from the subagent’s own messages. A rule can send a subagent elsewhere while its agent stays where it is.

Decisions are kept in memory for 24 hours after a conversation’s last request. Restarting magpie clears them, and the next message decides afresh.

## Reading the trace

The Routing tab shows each group’s latest request: who answered it, and under How the last request was routed, why.

The lines you can see about intent:

| The trace says | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| … was asked which of “A”, “B” turn 1 is, and said “B” (in 323 ms). | The classifier was asked, with these candidates, and named B. |
| … and said none (…). | It answered 0. |
| … (said before, for the same message). | The answer came from the 10-minute cache, so no call was made. |
| … was to tell which … but couldn’t — *reason* — so no rule with an intent matches it. | It failed. The reason is the error, the timeout, what it answered, or that it is resting after a failure. |
| Turn N begins and rule R matches — asks for “B” — so M goes first … | The rule that won, and the model put first. |
| Rule R matches, but M has no account or key that can take this request, so the group’s order stands. | No account or key for the rule’s model can take this request. |
| Rule R (…) sent turn N to M as it began; the turn stays there. | A tool round within the turn, held on its decision. |
| This turn began before magpie saw it, so the rules wait for the next one. | See *Waits* above. |

The classifier’s own calls appear in Usage under the agent *magpie*, with their tokens and cost, so you can see what classifying costs.

## Latency, cost, privacy

- **Latency..** Only the first request of a turn waits for the classifier, typically a few hundred milliseconds on a fast provider (323 ms in the screenshot) with a configured timeout of 8 seconds by default. Tool rounds within the turn, turns where no intent could decide, and cached answers add nothing.
- **Cost..** One short call per turn: roughly the size of your message plus the intents in, and one or two tokens out. In the example above that was 212 tokens in and 1 out. With a subscription model as the classifier, these calls count against that subscription’s limits.
- **Privacy..** The text of your message (up to about 4,000 characters) goes to the classifier’s provider. To keep it on your machine, use a local model from Ollama or LM Studio as the classifier. magpie keeps only a hash of the message and the answer, in memory, for 10 minutes. The message itself isn’t stored or logged.

## Writing good intents

- **Describe the request, not the model..** Write “writing or fixing tests”, not “hard tasks for Opus”. The classifier sees only your words and the message.
- **Keep kinds apart..** If two intents overlap (“a question”, “a question about the code”), a small model will choose between them unpredictably. Merge them, or make the difference plain.
- **Few and broad beats many and narrow..** Two to five intents are easy for an 8B model. Up to 200 characters each is allowed, but a few words are usually enough.
- **Order still matters..** Only the first matching rule counts, so put a rule that must win (such as a long-context rule) above the intent rules. The classifier is then skipped whenever that rule holds.
- **“None” is a real answer..** A turn that fits no intent goes to the group’s usual order, so let that order be your default choice.
- **Any language..** Intents and messages can be in any language the classifier understands. The fixed prompt is in English, and small models read mixed languages well.
- **Choosing a classifier..** Pick a small, fast model without reasoning: Llama 3.1 8B on Groq, a Flash-Lite, nano or mini model, Claude Haiku, DeepSeek’s non-reasoning chat model, or a local model. A reasoning model is slower; magpie asks it for its least reasoning and leaves it 2048 tokens, but a slow one can still miss the configured timeout. Check the trace for a few turns: if it guesses wrong, rewrite the intents before switching models.

## Numbers

| What | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Classifier timeout | 8 s by default; configurable from 1 to 60 s, including its provider’s failover |
| Rest after a failure | 30 s, per classifier model |
| Answer cache | 10 min, per classifier + intents + message; in memory |
| Turn decisions kept | 24 h after the conversation’s last request; in memory |
| Message sent | Up to 4,000 characters; longer is first 3,000 + last 1,000 |
| Classifier request | temperature 0, max_tokens 2048, the least reasoning the model has, not streamed |
| Intent length | Up to 200 characters; spaces collapsed, compared without case |
| Outgrown | At 95% of the current model’s context, only to a model with more |

## FAQ

### Is this embeddings or a vector search?

No. There is no embedding model, no similarity threshold, no keyword list and nothing to train. The classifier is an ordinary chat model that reads your intents and your message and answers with a number. It is only as good as that model and your wording, and the trace shows every answer.

### Does it look at the whole conversation?

No, only the message you just sent. So a follow-up like “now do the same for the other file” is judged on those words alone. Give that turn a clearer message, or add an intent that fits follow-ups.

### My agent made 40 requests for one message. Was the classifier asked 40 times?

No, once. The other 39 carried tool results, so they belong to the same turn and follow its decision. You can see this in the trace (“the turn stays there”) and in Usage (one *magpie* call).

### Can a turn switch models halfway?

Only in two cases: the model it is on fails and another member takes over, or the conversation outgrows the model’s context and a rule sends it to one with more room. Intent is never re-asked mid-turn.

### What if the classifier is down or slow?

The turn still goes through. After waiting up to the configured timeout (8 s by default), no intent matches and the group’s other rules and order decide. For the next 30 s magpie doesn’t ask that classifier again, so turns don’t each wait out the timeout. The trace gives the reason.

### Why did the turn not go to the rule’s model when the classifier named its intent?

Check the trace. The usual causes are:

- a rule above it matched first;
- another condition on the rule didn’t hold (tokens, images, reasoning or agent);
- no account or key for the rule’s model could take this request;
- it was a tool round in a turn that began elsewhere;
- magpie didn’t see the turn begin (“the rules wait”).

### Two rules have the same intent. What happens?

The intent is offered to the classifier once. If it is chosen, the first of those rules whose other conditions hold wins. Use this to send, for example, “writing or fixing tests” from Codex to one model and from Claude Code to another.

### Does changing a rule affect a turn already running?

No. Saving applies from the next turn. A turn whose rule you removed, or pointed at another model, keeps where it is until then; the trace says the rules wait.

### Can the classifier be a routing group, or one of the group’s own models?

It can’t be a group: it must be one model, `provider/model`, which magpie checks when you save. It can be any model magpie has, including one of the group’s members, a subscription model or a local model.

### Can I use a reasoning model?

Yes, if it answers within the configured timeout (8 s by default). magpie asks it for the least reasoning it has (`none`, else its lowest level) and leaves 2048 tokens, so thinking doesn’t crowd out the answer. A small, fast model is still the better choice: cheaper, and every turn waits for it.

### How well does it work with real models?

We ran 20 real coding messages (English and Chinese: quick questions, test work, and ordinary coding tasks, including “Fix the bug in parseTokens and add a test for it”) through a group with two intent rules. DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.3 Flash and MiMo v2.6 Flash each classified all 20 correctly; the median classifier time was 0.75 s, 1.3 s and 1.9 s. Gemini 3.8 Flash through one reseller took 11 s even at `low` reasoning, so with the default 8 s timeout every turn timed out and routed as if there were no intents — the trace said so each time. That is the pattern to expect: a wrong classifier costs you the routing, never the turn.

### Does retrying the same message ask again?

Not within 10 minutes: the same message with the same intents and the same classifier is answered from the cache, and the trace says “said before”. Changing an intent or the classifier makes it ask again.

### Which agents does it work with?

Any agent that sends to a routing group through magpie: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and the rest. Turns are detected from the request itself (a message with text and no tool results), whatever API the agent speaks.

### Is my message stored anywhere?

magpie keeps a hash of it (for the cache) and the classifier’s answer, in memory only. The text goes to the classifier’s provider, like any request, under that provider’s terms. The classifier’s usage record holds its token counts, not the text.

### How accurate is it?

That depends on the classifier and on how distinct your intents are. With a few clearly different kinds, a small model picks well; with overlapping ones it will sometimes guess. Since a wrong or missing answer only changes which model answers, start with two or three broad intents, watch the trace for a day and adjust the wording.

Questions or a setup worth sharing? Ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF). Routing groups in general are covered in [Get started](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/start#routing).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/masking

# Privacy masking

magpie can mask what your agents send before it leaves this computer. API keys, passwords and tokens, and when you ask, emails, phone numbers and words of your own, go to the vendor as placeholders such as `{{API_KEY_es6eu6jk}}`. In the reply each placeholder turns back into its value, so your agent and your files keep the real thing and the vendor never sees it. It runs on this computer, in magpie’s gateway, and is **off by default**.

> **It covers what goes through magpie.** An agent [connected to magpie](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/start) sends its requests through the gateway, and they are masked whichever provider or account answers. An agent that calls a vendor directly, not through magpie, is not covered.

## Turn it on

1. **Open the page.** Go to Settings → Privacy.
2. **Mask secrets.** Under What to mask, set Mask secrets to On: API keys, private keys, tokens and passwords.
3. **Personal data, if you want it.** Set Mask personal data to On for emails, phone numbers, ID and bank card numbers. Each further kind of personal data then gets its own switch below it.
4. **Your own words.** In Masked words, list names, codenames or hosts to keep from vendors, one on each row (several pasted with commas between become a row each). Masked words in any case makes *Nightjar* mask *NIGHTJAR* too. A secret magpie doesn’t know, such as your gateway’s own keys, goes under Masking rules: what it starts with, or a regular expression.
5. **Try it.** Paste a text into Try it to see exactly what the vendor would get. What you paste there isn’t kept.

It applies from the next request, with no restart and nothing to change in your agent. The work is done by the built-in plugin Privacy masking (`redact`, in Settings → Plugins), which is on whenever any masking is asked for.

There is no CLI command for it. Without the window (`magpie serve`, [Docker](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/docker)), open the same page with `magpie web`, or set it in `~/.config/magpie/settings.json` (`/config/magpie/settings.json` in Docker). The masker reads the file on every request:

```
{
  "redact": true,
  "redactPersonal": true,
  "redactWords": ["Nightjar", "db.acme-corp.cn"]
}
```

## What is masked

| Switch | What it finds |
| --- | --- |
| Mask secrets | Private key blocks (`-----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY-----`). API keys by their shape: `sk-…` (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter), `ghp_`/`github_pat_`, `glpat-`, `AIza…`, `xox…-`, `sk_live_`, `AKIA`/`ASIA`, `hf_`, `gsk_`, `xai-`, `npm_`, `pypi-`, `dop_v1_`, `SG.`, and relay keys like `oc_sk_…`. JWTs. The password in `user:password@host`. The value of a field named for a secret, as `.env` files and configs have them: `DB_PASSWORD=…`, `api_key: …`, `client_secret`, `token`, `credential`. Your own Masking rules. Wallet private keys by the shape their wallets export: a Bitcoin WIF, a BIP32 `xprv`, an Ethereum or TRON `0x` key, a Solana key or `id.json` keypair, a Sui `suiprivkey1…`, an Aptos `ed25519-priv-0x…`, a Stellar seed, a NEAR `ed25519:…` key, a Nostr `nsec1…`, an age identity, a Zcash extended spending key, and a 12 to 25 word seed phrase after *seed* or *mnemonic* whose every word is in the BIP39 list. A key with no prefix of its own is masked only when it checks out: a WIF or `xprv` by its checksum, a Solana key by its public half, a Stellar seed by its CRC, so a Solana transaction signature goes as written. A `0x` key has the shape of a transaction hash, so it is masked only after a key&rsquo;s name (`PRIVATE_KEY=`, `--private-key`, `new Wallet(…)`, 私钥); a hash, a storage slot or a sha256 sum goes as written. An exchange&rsquo;s API key, secret and `passphrase` go by their fields&rsquo; names. |
| Mask personal data | Emails, mainland China mobile numbers (not an 11-digit id: one under `order_id` or after 订单号 goes as written), Chinese ID numbers and bank card numbers whose checksum adds up. Also on by default: US Social Security numbers, passport numbers (after *passport*, 护照 or パスポート), IBANs, birthdays (next to *birthday*, *DOB* or 生日, and over a year ago, so today&rsquo;s date stays), MAC addresses and serial numbers (after *S/N*). Off until you turn them on, since agents send them in nearly every request: the user name in home folders (sent as a made-up name, the same every turn, so the model reads a real folder rather than a placeholder), user and computer names (`user@host`), public IP addresses (sent as a name such as `public-ip-kvxqmrtz`, so the model still knows the address is public and connects with it, and the real address goes back into its commands) and cloud storage buckets. A wallet or contract address (`0x` and 40 hex digits) is public and goes as written; a private key is still masked. |
| Masked words | Each word you listed, exactly, as `{{TERM_…}}`. A date, such as *1990-05-12*, matches that day however it is written: *1990/5/12*, *1990.05.12*, *1990年5月12日*, *19900512*, *May 12, 1990*, and *13/05/1990* style only where the day can’t be read as a month. Never another date or a version like *1990.5.12.1*. |
| Find with a local model | Under How it’s found. A model on this computer finds what no rule can: a name or an address in free text. It is on unless you turned it off, and AstrLink Guard downloads with the first masked request; until it is on disk, the rules mask alone. It needs Mask secrets or Mask personal data on, and finds under the same switches. The menu beside it picks the model: AstrLink Guard (Chinese and English, a 39 MB download, few false alarms in code, on a Mac it runs on the Neural Engine; the default) or OpenAI’s Privacy Filter (1.6 GB, uses the GPU, masks more ordinary values in code). Confidence threshold under it is how sure the model must be before a value is masked: Privacy Filter’s default is 0.5, AstrLink Guard’s 0.8, its publisher’s. Higher masks fewer ordinary values, and lets more real names and addresses through: the rules after the model drop most false alarms already, so the default is where we measured the fewest real values lost. |

A placeholder is the kind plus eight characters of a keyed hash. The same value gets the same placeholder every time, so the conversation reads the same turn after turn and the vendor’s prompt cache stays valid. The values are held in memory only.

## An example

With Mask secrets and Mask personal data on and *Nightjar* in Masked words, your agent sends:

```
Deploy Nightjar with OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-8fK2mQx7Lp4Rt9Vw3Yz6Ab1Cd, then mail li.wei@acme-corp.cn or call 13800138000.
```

```
Deploy {{TERM_5hmsrhdc}} with OPENAI_API_KEY={{API_KEY_srhjgvja}}, then mail {{EMAIL_eh5um6mb}} or call {{PHONE_uf7iy2qq}}.
```

When the model answers *“I set OPENAI_API_KEY to {{API_KEY_srhjgvja}} in .env”*, your agent reads the real key there, in streamed text and tool-call arguments alike, so the file it writes has the real key. A placeholder the model rewrote a little (spaces inside the braces, another case) is still turned back.

## Check that it works

- **Before:.** Try it on Settings → Privacy shows the text as the vendor would get it, with each value’s kind.
- **Each request:.** a shield badge with a count appears on the request in the Gateway page’s recent calls and in the Routing log. Point at it for the kinds; click it to open the request’s record.
- **Over time:.** Insights → Masking (also What was masked on the Privacy page) shows the values masked over 7 or 30 days by kind, agent and provider, and each request’s text as the vendor saw it, placeholders marked.

The records are kept in `~/.config/magpie/masking` for 30 days: the agent, provider, model, and each placeholder’s kind, length and first characters, never the value.

## When a value is found

Under When a value is found, choose per kind:

- Mask (the default): sent as a placeholder.
- Warn: sent as written, and the badge counts it in amber.
- Block: the request is held back with a 400, *“magpie held this request back: Settings › Privacy blocks API_KEY, and it has one (sk-…, 33 characters). Nothing was sent.”* The message never has the value.

A value the task needs as it is, such as a team address or a test key, goes in Never mask: it is sent as written wherever it is found whole.

## What it leaves alone, and limits

- **Thinking stays as the vendor wrote it..** A thinking block with its signature, Gemini’s thoughts and Responses’ encrypted reasoning are sealed by the vendor and go back unchanged, so the signature still matches. Only values already masked elsewhere in the request are swapped in them.
- **Ids and tool definitions go as written:.** model ids, message and call ids, UUIDs, tool names, MCP server names, and tool schemas (their descriptions are masked), so a vendor or a tool can still check them.
- **Images and file data are sent as they are..** Text inside a screenshot is not masked.
- **It fails closed..** If masking is on and can’t run (the Privacy masking plugin turned off by hand, or the local model you turned on can’t answer), the request gets a 503 that says nothing was sent. It is never sent unmasked instead. The model on by default that can’t answer leaves the rules to mask alone.
- **A provider can skip it..** Send requests unmasked on a provider sends its requests as written: a model on this computer or your local network (Ollama, LM Studio), and, if you choose, any other provider, a subscription or a plugin’s provider too. Turned on for one that isn’t local, the editor says its vendor gets your requests unmasked. A request that can fall back to a provider still masked is masked. `magpie provider set ollama unmasked=yes` does the same.
- **Or send what masking would change to one of them..** In Settings › Privacy, Instead of masking, send to picks such a model. An agent’s request that masking would change then goes to it as written, so it can answer about the real names, and a request with nothing to mask goes where it was going. If that model fails, the request fails: it is never masked and sent to a vendor instead. Off by default.
- **The model sees placeholders..** It can’t read or reason about a masked value; it can only pass it on. Put a value it must read under Never mask.
- **Rules find shapes..** A phone number in another country’s format or a name in free text needs Find with a local model, or your own Masked words and Masking rules. Try your own text in Try it first.

See also [Privacy](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/privacy) for everything magpie sends by itself. The code is [internal/redact](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/tree/main/internal/redact) and [internal/masking](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/blob/main/internal/masking/masking.go).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/troubleshooting

# Fixing common errors: 401, 429, 502, 504 and more

An error from magpie’s gateway says what went wrong in its own words. This page lists the common ones, what causes them, and the fix.

Every request is listed on magpie’s Routing page, with which provider and account it went to and how each try ended. Copy Report on a request copies what you need to ask for help.

## 401 and 403: a key or sign-in refused

**From the vendor.** The provider turned down the key or sign-in magpie sent. magpie sets that key or account aside and tries the next one, so you see the error only when none is left. A sign-in that has run out says so, for example “the ChatGPT sign-in has expired — sign in again”.

- **Fix:.** sign in again from ＋ Add provider (or `magpie accounts add <provider>`), or give the provider a new key.

**From magpie itself.** magpie answers 403 on its own in a few cases, before anything is sent:

| Error | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| model disabled | You turned the model off in magpie. | Turn it on again on its provider. |
| model not allowed for the gateway key | The gateway key is held to some models. | `magpie gateway-key models <id>` lists or changes them. |
| magpie doesn’t answer the web page … | A web page called the gateway from a browser. | List it in Settings › Network and sharing › Web pages, and send a gateway key. |

## 429 and rest periods

A 429 means the provider is out of quota, out of credit or rate limiting you. magpie rests the key or account that was refused and sends the request to the next account, the next member of a routing group, or the provider’s Fallback. The provider’s row shows Resting · {why} · back at {time}.

| Refused for | Rests |
| --- | --- |
| Quota, with a reset time | Until the reset |
| Rate limit, with Retry-After | Until then |
| Credit | 30 minutes, then 2 hours, 8 hours, a day, 3 days and a week if it is refused again |
| A ChatGPT account out of credits | Until the reset its refusal names, else until its full window renews, else 5 hours |
| Any other failure | A minute, doubling on repeats up to 10 minutes (30 for a rate limit) |

- **Ask it again now..** Try now ends the rest: the next request asks it again. Refused again, it rests again.
- **Cap the rest..** `magpie provider rest-cap <id> 4h` sets the longest rest for a provider; `off` stops it resting for failures that say nothing of why.
- **A relay whose limits pass in a moment..** Untick Set it aside when out of quota or rate limited in the provider editor’s Advanced: a 429 then rests nothing, and the next request goes to it as usual.
- **Never all at once..** Add a second account or a fallback model, so a spent one never stops the agent. `magpie accounts` shows how much of each account’s allowance is used.

Rests are kept across restarts, so quitting magpie doesn’t bring a resting account back early.

## 502: the provider didn’t answer

A 502 means magpie couldn’t get an API reply from the provider. What follows the provider’s name says which case it is:

- **“didn’t answer: …”.** The connection failed: a name that doesn’t resolve, a refused connection, a proxy that is down. When this computer has no network at all, magpie notices and rests nobody.
- **“… not an API reply”.** The provider answered, but with a web page (a sign-in page, a Cloudflare challenge), nothing at all, or something that isn’t JSON. The base URL usually points at a web site instead of the API: check it against the vendor’s docs, and whether it should end in `/v1`.
- **OpenCode: “… which is no error, not an API reply”..** OpenCode’s gateway sometimes answers a 400 holding only the model’s name. The same request is answered some seconds later, so magpie reads it as a 502, asks again within the request’s patience or tries a group’s next member, and rests nobody. It is tied to requests carrying very large tool lists.

A 502, 503, 504, 529 or Cloudflare’s 520 to 524 counts as busy: magpie asks again or moves to a routing group’s next member before the agent sees it.

## 504: no answer in time

- **“<provider>: no first token in Ns”..** A routing group gives each member a time to start answering (First token). The member was slower, so the next was asked. Raise it on the group for a slow model.
- **“no member of the group answered within its Ns budget”..** Every member of the group was tried within the group’s time and none answered.
- **“magpie held this request for … without routing it to any provider”..** The request waited inside magpie and was stopped rather than left waiting. Send it again; if it comes back, Copy Report on that request on the Routing page and share it.

## Model not found (404)

The error reads *magpie knows no model “…”*, often with *did you mean …?* and the list of your provider ids.

- **Name it as magpie does..** Use `provider/model`, as `magpie models` lists it, a routing group’s id or name, or a bare model id.
- **“… is switched off in Magpie, so … is not served”..** The provider or routing group is off. Switch it on again on the Providers or Routing page.
- **No providers yet..** The error says “add a provider in magpie first”.

## The agent doesn’t show the model

- **Restart the agent..** Most agents read their config only when they start. magpie says so on the agent’s row after a change, for example “Codex builds its model list at start-up”. Codex’s app also keeps an app-server running; restart it as the notice says.
- **Check magpie serves it..** `magpie models` lists every model you can pick. A model you turned off, or one whose provider is switched off, isn’t listed.
- **Claude Code..** `/model` lists magpie’s models marked “via magpie”. If `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` or `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX` is set in your shell, Claude Code goes to that cloud instead of magpie; remove it from your shell profile.

## Port 3425 is in use

The gateway listens on `127.0.0.1:3425`. To move it, open Settings › Network and sharing › Gateway address. Only the port is set there, 1024 to 65535, and the agents magpie connected move with it.

| magpie says | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Port … is in use by another program: pick another one | Pick a free port. |
| Another magpie serves the gateway at …: set its port there, or quit it first | Two copies of magpie are running. Quit one. |
| Port … is taken by another program, magpie web perhaps: magpie tries again every few seconds | Find what holds the port, or move the gateway to another. |
| MAGPIE_ADDR=… sets the gateway’s whole address, host:port: unset it to set the port here | Unset `MAGPIE_ADDR`, or change it. |

## Agents in WSL

On Windows, magpie looks in running WSL distros for agents such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Kimi Code and Qwen Code. Each one it finds gets a row of its own on the Agents page, and magpie sets it up as it does on Windows. It never starts a stopped distro.

- **The agent isn’t listed..** Start the distro, and check Settings › General › Detect agents in WSL is on.
- **It can’t reach magpie..** Under WSL’s default NAT networking, magpie also serves the gateway at Windows’ address on the WSL network, with a key of its own, and writes that address into the agent’s config. With mirrored networking the agent uses `127.0.0.1` as on Windows. Windows’ firewall still decides: WSL’s network counts as Public, so allow magpie there if the connection is blocked.
- **A change doesn’t show..** An agent in WSL reads its config at start-up: restart it there.

## From another computer on the network

By default the gateway answers only this computer. To use it from another: Settings › Network and sharing › Share on local network. The other computer sends a gateway key from the Gateway page’s Gateway keys.

- **“magpie isn’t shared on the local network”..** Turn sharing on, on the computer that runs magpie.
- **401..** The key is missing, off or expired. Send an enabled gateway key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>` or `x-api-key`.
- **403 for a model..** The key is held to some models: `magpie gateway-key models <id>`.

Don’t open the port to the internet; use a VPN between your computers. The full setup, another magpie included, is in [Remote magpie](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/remote).

## A subscription moved to a plugin isn’t served

Command Code, Cursor, Devin, Factory, Grok, Kiro, Xiaomi MiMo, Qoder, WorkBuddy, ZCode and Zed are no longer built into magpie. Each is served by a community plugin that does the same job. Accounts added before still need to move to the plugin, and nothing serves them until they do.

- **Fix:.** a line over the Providers list says “… built-in subscription is retired, and its accounts haven’t moved to its plugin yet”. Press Move to the plugin: magpie installs the plugin and checks each account. Moving keeps your accounts, models and agents as they are. magpie also moves them by itself, and installing the plugin from the Plugins page does too.

An error after the move comes from the plugin, which does the sign-in, models and requests.

## FAQ

### Why does magpie answer 502 when the provider is up?

The provider answered with something that isn’t an API reply, such as a web page or an empty body. The base URL usually points at the vendor’s web site instead of its API.

### Why does an account stay unused after a 429?

magpie rests it until the reset the vendor named, or for a while if none was named. The provider’s row says when it is back, and Try now ends the rest.

### What does “magpie knows no model” mean?

No provider serves a model by that name. Name it as provider/model, as magpie models lists it, or switch its provider on again.

### How do I change magpie’s port?

Settings › Network and sharing › Gateway address. The agents magpie connected move with it.

### Can an agent in WSL use magpie on Windows?

Yes. magpie finds agents in running WSL distros and sets each up with an address it can reach. Under NAT networking, Windows’ firewall must let WSL’s connection through.

### Can I use magpie from another computer?

Yes. Turn on Settings › Network and sharing › Share on local network, and send a gateway key from the other computer. Don’t open the port to the internet.

Still stuck? Copy the request’s report from the Routing page and ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/library

# Library

magpie’s Library keeps instructions, MCP servers, skills, hooks and subagents in one place, and writes each of them into every agent you tick for it, in that agent’s own files and format. The agents read those files as they always do. magpie adds no layer between an agent and what it is given: the agent itself decides when to use a skill, an MCP tool or a subagent.

The page has seven tabs: Instructions, MCP servers, Skills, Hooks, Subagents, RTK and billion-context. Each item has a row of agents; tick an agent to give it the item, untick it to take it away. An agent reads the change when it starts again.

## Where it is kept

- **The library.** is `library.json` in magpie’s config folder (`~/.config/magpie`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/magpie` when that is set). Instruction texts and skill folders are in `library/` next to it.
- **Every change.** saves the library and writes it into every agent at once. magpie records what it wrote, so it only ever takes away its own entries and leaves yours alone.
- **Backups..** Before a change, the files it replaces are copied to `backups/` in the same folder. The last 30 are kept. The Backups button at the top of each tab opens them.
- **Write it again..** After you install an agent, or edit its files by hand, `magpie library sync` writes the library into every agent again.

```
magpie library          # what the library gives each agent
magpie library sync     # write it into the agents again
```

## Instructions

Instructions are text every session of an agent starts with, such as house rules or a coding style. magpie writes its part between two marker lines in the agent’s instructions file:

```
<!-- magpie:begin · written by magpie from its Library -->
…the Library's instructions…
<!-- magpie:end -->
```

Everything outside the markers is yours and is never changed. You can keep several named sets and give each set to different agents, and a set can live in a file of your own.

| Agent | File |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` (or `AGENTS.override.md` when you use one) |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini/config/GEMINI.md` |
| OpenCode | `AGENTS.md` in its config folder |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md` |
| Goose, Crush, Qwen Code, CodeBuddy | `.goosehints`, `CRUSH.md`, `QWEN.md`, `CODEBUDDY.md` |
| Droid, Grok, dsh, omp | `AGENTS.md` in the agent’s own folder |
| Pi, OmO | the first one there of `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` |

Folders follow the agent’s own setting: a custom `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `CODEX_HOME` is used in place of the default.

## MCP servers

An MCP server is either a command (a program the agent starts, such as `npx …`) or a URL (HTTP or SSE). magpie writes one entry per server into each ticked agent’s MCP config, in that agent’s format, and keeps any fields you added to the entry yourself.

| Agent | File |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude.json` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/settings.json` |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` |
| OpenCode | `opencode.json` |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` |
| Zed | `context_servers` in its `settings.json` |

- **Variables..** `${NAME}` in a header or an env value is written in each agent’s own syntax. An agent that has no such syntax is not given that server, and the page says why.
- **SSE..** Codex, Goose, dsh, Grok, Command Code and Zed can’t use an SSE server. Claude Desktop takes no remote servers at all.
- **Single tools off..** You can turn off tools one by one for Codex, Gemini CLI, Crush, Hermes Agent, Claude Code and OpenCode, each in its own setting. Every other agent gets the whole server.
- **Sign-in..** A server that needs OAuth is signed in to once, in magpie. Agents then reach it through magpie’s gateway at `/mcp/<name>`.
- **This computer only..** Turn off Sync to your other computers for a server that should stay here (`magpie library mcp local <name> on`).

With the [MCP router](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/mcp-router) on, each agent gets one server named `magpie` in place of these entries, and magpie runs each command server once for all of them. It is off by default.

## Skills

A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` in it. The agent reads each skill’s name and description and loads the rest when a task needs it. Add one from GitHub, any git repository, a folder on this computer, or the market on the Skills tab.

| Agent | Folder |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/skills` |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/skills` |
| OpenCode | `skills` in its config folder |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/skills` |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/skills` |
| Goose | `~/.agents/skills` |

### Links or copies

Give skills as sets how a skill reaches an agent, for every agent or, under By agent, for one:

- **Links.** (the default). The agent’s folder links to the library’s copy, so an update reaches every agent at once. On Windows without the right to make links, a junction is used.
- **Copies..** Each agent gets a folder of its own, for tools that don’t follow links. A copy is made again when the library’s skill changes. If the agent, or you, edit a copy, the next sync takes the newest edit into the library and gives it to the other agents. An edit that loses to a newer one is kept with the backups.

A skill folder of your own with the same name is never written over: the page asks whether to use the library’s or keep yours.

### Editing and updates

- **Edit.** opens a skill’s files on the page; Save (or ⌘S) writes them. The command line has no editor.
- **Updates..** When you open the Skills tab, skills from GitHub are checked for updates if 12 hours have passed since the last check (`magpie library skill update` checks now). A skill you changed is never replaced without asking.
- **Put skills in..** Skills go to each ticked agent’s own folder (the default), or also into `~/.agents/skills`, which Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Crush, Droid, Kimi Code and other tools read.
- **Off here..** A skill can be turned off on this computer only; a sync from another computer doesn’t turn it back on.

## Subagents

A subagent is a helper the main agent can hand a task to. It has a name, a description and a prompt. magpie writes it as a file in each ticked agent’s subagent folder. The main agent reads every subagent’s **description** and decides itself when to call one, so the description should say plainly what it is for and when to use it.

- **Name:.** 2 to 50 lowercase letters, digits and `-`. A few names are reserved, such as `default` and `main`.
- **Description:.** required, up to 1,000 characters.
- **Prompt:.** required. It becomes the subagent’s instructions.
- **Model:.** optional. See Subagent models.

| Agent | File | Skills, MCP servers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/agents/<name>.md` | the ones you pick |
| Codex | `~/.codex/agents/<name>.toml` | all the agent has |
| OpenCode | `agents/<name>.md` in its config folder | all the agent has |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/agents/<name>.md` | all the agent has |
| Qwen Code | `agents/<name>.md` in its folder | all the agent has |
| Droid | `~/.factory/droids/<name>.md` | MCP servers you pick; all skills |
| Grok | `agents/<name>.md` in its folder | all the agent has |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/agents/<name>.md` | all the agent has |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/agents/<name>.agent.md` | all the agent has |

- Only Claude Code limits a subagent to the skills you pick, and only Claude Code and Droid to the MCP servers you pick. Elsewhere a subagent has everything its agent has.
- Cursor: only the Cursor app reads `~/.cursor/agents`. `cursor-agent` reads only a project’s `.cursor/agents`.
- Kimi Code, Goose, Crush, Qoder, CodeBuddy, iFlow and Kiro have no user-wide subagent folder, so they get none. Agents in WSL get none either.
- If you edit a file magpie wrote, it becomes yours and magpie stops changing it. A file of your own with the same name is never written over; the page shows a problem instead.

## Subagent models

A subagent’s Model field is written only for **Codex**. Every other agent runs its subagents on the model it picks itself, and the page says so. Left empty, the field reads Picked by the agent.

For Codex, the model goes into the subagent’s `.toml` file. Codex lays that file over the spawn, so requests carry that model and magpie’s gateway routes them like any other request. You can pick any model in Codex’s list, a magpie `provider/model`, or a routing group (`group/<id>`).

### Codex’s subagent model on the Agents page

Codex’s row on the Agents page has a subagent model of its own, for every subagent Codex starts:

- **Lead’s pick.** (the default). The main agent picks each subagent’s model, one of Codex’s own too. A subagent it names no model for runs on the main agent’s model. A resumed subagent stays on the model it started on.
- **Same as the lead..** Every subagent runs on the main agent’s model.
- **A model or a group..** Every subagent runs on it, even when the main agent names another.

> **The Agents page wins.** When that setting is anything but Lead’s pick, the gateway sends every Codex subagent request to it, over a Library subagent’s own model too. The Library editor then says so. Picking a model there also removes `default_subagent_model` from Codex’s config.

Codex’s own `[agents] default_subagent_model` in `config.toml` is a different thing: only the model a subagent starts on when the main agent names none. One exception to all of the above: a task the ChatGPT backend has sealed stays on the model it asked for, unless the setting is a ChatGPT account’s model.
